title: Brain-computer interface enables independent, accurate communication for man living with ALS
summary: Casey Harrell, a 47-year-old man with ALS, independently used a BrainGate2 intracortical BCI at home for nearly two years, accumulating over 3,800 hours of use and communicating more than 183,000 sentences at 56 words per minute with greater than 99% word accuracy. Published in Nature Medicine, the study is the first to demonstrate a high-performance BCI operating reliably as a daily assistive tool outside a controlled clinical setting.

title: China has approved the world's first invasive brain-computer chip
summary: China's National Medical Products Administration granted commercial approval to NEO, a BCI from Neuracle Technology and Tsinghua University, making it the first invasive BCI cleared for commercial sale anywhere in the world. The coin-sized device rests on the dura mater rather than piercing the cortex and decodes movement intentions to help paralyzed patients regain motor function, beating Neuralink to commercial approval.

title: A brain-computer interface that works with, not against, the brain
summary: Yale researchers built a real-time fMRI BCI that learns to align with the brain's natural activity patterns rather than requiring users to perform arbitrary mental tasks. In gaming experiments, participants controlled games more intuitively and with less cognitive effort, establishing a new design philosophy that could make BCIs more accessible across varying neurological profiles.

title: Neuralink launches VOICE trial: speech restoration targeting conversational speeds
summary: Neuralink began enrolling participants in its VOICE clinical trial, targeting speech restoration for ALS and stroke patients by decoding signals from speech-production brain regions. Participant Kenneth Shock demonstrated early speech output via the implant, with the trial aiming for real-time conversational speeds of 140 words per minute.

title: The frontier of brain science: AI and organoid research takes center stage in Silicon Valley
summary: A Silicon Valley gathering convened UC Santa Cruz and partner researchers to plan a platform combining AI with living brain organoids to decode how neural circuits form and fail. The group aims to scale to thousands of simultaneously grown organoids within two years, using AI to identify where connections go awry in neurological diseases such as autism and schizophrenia.

title: Computing with Living Neurons: Chaos-Controlled Reservoir Computing with Knowledge Transplant
summary: Researchers demonstrated that biological neuron cultures operating in a chaotic dynamic regime can reliably perform reservoir computing tasks, and introduced a knowledge transplant technique that transfers learned computational patterns between separate neuron cultures without retraining. The work provides a path toward modular, reusable wetware computing systems bridging organoid intelligence and spiking network dynamics.

title: Living brain-cell biocomputers are now training on dopamine
summary: Swiss company FinalSpark demonstrated that their cloud-accessible bioprocessing platform can train organoid networks using dopamine as a reward signal, replicating biological reinforcement learning in a wetware system. This proof-of-concept shows that biologically plausible feedback mechanisms can drive learning in lab-grown neural tissue, moving wetware computing closer to self-improving systems.

title: Bridging the gap between neuromorphic ionic computing and more efficient AI
summary: Researchers developed new material systems coupling biological-style ionic processing with silicon neuromorphic chips, achieving sub-100 mV switching voltages and femtojoule-level energy consumption per operation. The work closes a long-standing efficiency gap between ion-based neuromorphic devices and conventional AI accelerators, pointing toward ultra-low-power edge inference hardware inspired by how neurons communicate.

title: Behavioral timescale synaptic plasticity: properties, elements and functions
summary: A Nature Neuroscience paper characterizes behavioral timescale synaptic plasticity (BTSP), a newly discovered form of hippocampal synaptic change that operates over seconds rather than the milliseconds of classical STDP. Triggered by single dendritic plateau potentials, BTSP can generate new place cells in just one trial, offering a biologically plausible mechanism for rapid spatial learning that challenges existing models of memory formation.

title: Role of the hippocampus in systems consolidation of remote fear memory
summary: A study in Experimental & Molecular Medicine challenges classical systems consolidation theory by showing that the hippocampus remains directly active during recall of remote (temporally distant) fear memories, not just recent ones. The hippocampus actively distributes memory content across cortical regions throughout consolidation, fundamentally revising models of how the brain achieves long-term memory storage.

title: Prosthetic leg with neural sensory feedback shows clinical benefits for amputees
summary: ETH Zurich and startup SensArs Neuroprosthetics developed a lower-limb prosthesis that delivers tactile sensations by electrically stimulating residual nerves in the thigh, giving amputees genuine sensory feedback from their prosthetic foot. Clinical trials showed patients walked farther and more stably than with standard prosthetics, while reporting significant reductions in phantom limb pain.

title: Local brain connectome parameters across the spectrum of clinical cognitive decline
summary: A Frontiers in Neuroscience study mapped local connectome parameters — node degree, clustering coefficient, and global efficiency — across patients spanning healthy aging through mild cognitive impairment to Alzheimer's disease. The authors identified specific circuit metrics that reliably track the clinical continuum of cognitive decline, providing potential quantitative biomarkers for earlier neurodegeneration diagnosis.

title: Peking University's phase-change memristor chip reconstructs brain surfaces in milliseconds
summary: Chinese researchers at Peking University built a new computer chip that mimics how the brain's memory and processing work together, using a material called phase-change memristors. In tests, the chip reconstructed detailed 3D maps of brain surfaces up to 478 times faster than a top-tier graphics card, hinting at faster tools for brain-computer interfaces and diagnosing brain disease.

title: Sound-wave computer chip mimics how brain synapses learn
summary: Engineers at the University of Arizona built a computer chip that processes information using sound waves instead of electricity, mimicking how brain synapses strengthen or weaken over time. The device, called a topological acoustic synapse, can copy both fast, dopamine-like learning signals and slow, long-term stress responses while using far less power than standard electronic chips.

title: Brain-inspired chip design splits "fast" and "slow" memory like the cortex does
summary: Researchers at Imperial College London and ETH Zurich designed a brain-inspired chip architecture that separates fast, spike-based signals from a slower memory pathway, mirroring how real neurons balance quick reactions with longer-term context. The design cut power use roughly 5-fold and needed 40-60% fewer parameters than previous spiking neural network chips while running up to 4 times faster.

title: First complete wiring map of an entire fruit fly nervous system
summary: An international team led by Harvard and Princeton finished mapping every connection between neurons in an adult fruit fly's entire nervous system, linking the brain to the nerve cord for the first time. The map shows the fly's movements are controlled by many small, local circuits working together rather than one central "command center," offering clues about how brains in general organize behavior.

title: Scientists map the brain circuit linking deep sleep to growth hormone release
summary: Scientists mapped the brain circuit that connects deep sleep to the release of growth hormone, showing the two processes regulate each other in a feedback loop. The discovery helps explain why poor sleep can hurt muscle repair, fat metabolism, and brain health, and could point toward new treatments for sleep and metabolic disorders.

title: Brain keeps processing language even under general anesthesia
summary: Baylor College of Medicine researchers recorded brain activity in surgery patients under general anesthesia and found their hippocampus kept processing spoken language, distinguishing sounds and even anticipating upcoming words. The findings suggest the anesthetized brain stays far more active than assumed, even though patients typically don't consciously remember any of it.

title: A specific set of hippocampus neurons is required to remember new acquaintances
summary: Researchers found that a specific set of neurons in the hippocampus that connect to the brain's cortex are essential for turning short-term memories of new acquaintances into lasting ones. Turning off these neurons in mice disrupted their ability to remember newly met individuals, while memories of already-familiar companions stayed intact.

title: China performs the world's first commercial brain-computer interface implant
summary: Chinese firm Neuracle Technology and Tsinghua University implanted their NEO brain-computer interface in a patient with a decade-old spinal cord injury, the first surgery since NEO won commercial regulatory approval in March. The coin-sized, 8-electrode device sits on top of the brain's protective membrane and lets the patient drive a robotic glove to attempt grasping motions.

title: Paralyzed woman in China controls a computer cursor with her thoughts
summary: A 26-year-old paralyzed woman in Jiangsu Province, China moved a computer cursor using only her thoughts, one month after surgeons at the Affiliated Hospital of Nantong University implanted an invasive brain-computer interface. It's an early sign she may progress to more complex digital tasks as her control improves.

title: Intensive practice physically rewires the brain to enable true multitasking
summary: Georgetown University researchers found that extensive practice moves well-rehearsed tasks out of the prefrontal cortex and into dedicated circuits, freeing the brain's central 'thinking' hub to handle a second task at the same time. It's direct neural evidence that automaticity from practice enables genuine parallel processing, not just fast task-switching.

title: Study finds the brain begins learning to identify new objects by reshaping how it sees them
summary: MIT McGovern Institute and York University researchers combined brain recordings with computational modeling to show that learning to distinguish new object categories reshapes the visual cortex's own representations, not just later decision-making. The models predicted resulting perceptual changes that matched observed behavior.

title: Brain regions once thought purely passive turn out to help make decisions early on
summary: University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign researchers found that primary sensory brain regions are shaped by rapid feedback from higher-order areas much earlier in decision-making than the classical feedforward model predicted. The finding, published in PNAS, suggests perception and choice are far more intertwined than assumed.

title: A cerebellum-inspired chip spots anomalies almost instantly while barely using any power
summary: Northwestern University engineers built a molybdenum disulfide 'memtransistor' that mimics the cerebellum's excitatory/inhibitory balance to stay dormant on routine data and react only to genuine anomalies. It caught abnormal heartbeats within a fifth of a heartbeat at over 98% accuracy using about 10,000 times fewer computing operations than standard approaches.

title: Your fingers may hold a secret of human brain evolution
summary: A study of 225 newborns found that finger-length patterns linked to higher prenatal estrogen exposure predicted larger head circumference in boys, but not girls. It's new population-level evidence for the hypothesis that shifts in prenatal hormone exposure helped drive human brain expansion.

title: Estrogen in the first six weeks of pregnancy may set a baby boy's brain size at birth
summary: Direct blood measurements of maternal estrogen at 6-8 weeks gestation in 47 mother-infant pairs positively predicted neonatal head circumference, with a stronger effect in male infants. It independently confirms a companion finger-length study, converging on the same early-pregnancy hormone link to brain size.

title: The hidden skeleton "gatekeeper" inside brain cells could help fight Alzheimer's
summary: Penn State researchers identified a cytoskeletal structure inside neurons that regulates endocytosis; when it weakens, neurons rapidly absorb toxic proteins linked to Alzheimer's. Stabilizing this structural gatekeeper could become a new preventive strategy distinct from clearing plaques after the fact.

title: How LSD reshapes brain circuitry to blur the lines between perception and thought
summary: Brain imaging and computational modeling showed LSD boosts neural synchronization and shifts excitation/inhibition balance in cortical circuits, blurring the boundary between sensory processing and abstract thought. It's a mechanistic, circuit-level account of how the drug alters perception.

title: Oxide-based chip element merges processing and memory, advancing neuromorphic computing
summary: Brazilian researchers (UFSCar) built a single oxide-heterostructure device that can act as a transistor, memristor, or memcapacitor, merging memory and processing in one physical element. A demo circuit used it for digit recognition via physical reservoir computing.
